description:
We are team Planet MS'X: Marti (10) and Santi (9) from Uruguay!

We built Sky Detectives, a detective game where anyone can investigate the sky with real NASA SPHEREx images: pick a suspect, watch the photos blink and decide if it's a planet.

It's Santi's fourth Space Apps (2025 Global Nominee for Uruguay): he codes the game. It's Marti's first: she drew every suspect by hand.

Two kids, five suspects, real NASA data. Case open!
summary:
In 1930, Pluto was discovered by blinking two photos of the sky and spotting the one dot that moved. Today, NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the whole sky every six months: far too many images for anyone to check alone. Sky Detectives turns that search into a detective game anyone can play.

Players pick one of five suspects, the five target objects of the Planet X & SPHEREx challenge. The game downloads real SPHEREx images of that spot taken on different dates, blinks them like a flipbook, and builds a difference image where anything that moved appears as a black-and-white pair. Then it measures the motion and checks it against the SIMBAD catalog: for Epsilon Indi B, we measured 4.7 arcseconds per year, the same value astronomers report. Players earn XP by solving detective challenges, and every case ends with the question at the heart of the challenge: is it a planet?

Sky Detectives lets kids do real science instead of just reading about it. Made in Uruguay by Santi (9), who programmed it, and Marti (10), who drew every suspect.
details:
WHY WE CHOSE THIS CHALLENGE

In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by blinking two photographs of the same patch of sky and spotting the one dot that jumped. Almost a hundred years later, the Planet X & SPHEREx challenge asks the same question with a new telescope: what moves, and what changes, in the sky? We chose it because the core idea is something every kid already knows how to do: spot the difference between two pictures. We wanted to show that the method that found a planet can be played by anyone. There is also a real need behind it: SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months, and no one can look at all those images alone. More eyes help, and kids have very good eyes for spotting differences.

TEAM
Santi (9) programmed and tested the game. This is his fourth NASA Space Apps Challenge; in 2025 his project was a Global Nominee for Uruguay. Marti (10) created all the characters: she drew them by hand, and they were then digitized and enhanced with Canva's AI tools. This is Marti's first NASA Space Apps Challenge.

IN OUR OWN WORDS

"For me, the hardest part was improving the game by thinking of improvements that are really useful. I would tell other kids it's a pretty good topic, and that you could spend weeks working on it, like we did." — Santi, 9

WHAT IT DOES

Sky Detectives is a desktop game that turns NASA SPHEREx data into detective cases. The player opens a detective notebook with five suspects, some of them move across the sky; others change their brightness:

  • Barnard's Star ("The Runner")
  • Epsilon Indi B ("The Twins")
  • WISE 0855 ("The Cold Ghost")
  • RW Aurigae ("The Blinking Baby")
  • R Draconis ("The Giant Heart")

HOW IT WORKS

  1. The game looks up each suspect's position and motion in the SIMBAD catalog and works out where it is today.
  2. It searches the IRSA archive for SPHEREx images of that spot taken on different dates, in the infrared detector the player chooses.
  3. The images blink like a flipbook, and the game subtracts the first image from the last: anything that moved appears as a black-and-white pair.
  4. It measures how far the suspect moved (or how much its brightness changed) and compares the result with the catalog.
  5. The player solves a detective challenge (point at the suspect, say what it did or which way it moved) and earns XP, then gives a final verdict: is it a planet?

RESULT

For Epsilon Indi B, the game measured 1.05 pixels of motion in 1.40 years: 4.7 arcseconds per year, matching the catalog value of 4.7 arcseconds per year (1% difference; values rounded).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

  • Real science, not a simulation. Every sky image in the game is a real SPHEREx observation downloaded from NASA's IRSA archive, and every result is checked against the SIMBAD catalog that professional astronomers use.
  • Anyone can be an astronomer. No telescope, no expert knowledge and no prior astronomy classes are needed: if you can spot a difference, you can investigate the sky.
  • It teaches how science really works. The game doesn't just give answers. If a measurement doesn't match the catalog, it reports a "doubtful clue" instead of declaring the case solved. If a suspect is invisible in one detector, it tells the player to try another one, which shows that each infrared detector sees a different kind of light.
  • It teaches why, not just what. After each verdict, the game explains why the suspect is or isn't a planet: a star shines with its own light; a brown dwarf is too heavy to be a planet.
  • Learning by playing. Challenges, XP and a final verdict keep kids engaged long enough to really look at the data.
  • Reliable in classrooms. The game saves the images it downloads, so it keeps working even when the archive is busy.
  • Cross-checking with a second witness. A button opens NASA WISE images of the same suspect, so players can confirm the motion with another telescope, just like real astronomers do. Next, we want to add Canada's NEOSSAT as a third witness.
  • Inspiring other kids. Sky Detectives was made by a 9-year-old and a 10-year-old. If they can catch moving stars, anyone can.

CREATIVITY

We took the oldest trick in planet hunting and turned it into a detective story. Each object is a suspect with a personality that matches its science: Barnard's Star is "The Runner" because it crosses the sky faster than any other star; Epsilon Indi B is "The Twins," two brown dwarfs travelling together; WISE 0855 is "The Cold Ghost," almost invisible because it is as cold as a freezer; RW Aurigae is "The Blinking Baby," a newborn star hidden by dust; and R Draconis is "The Giant Heart," an old star that swells and shrinks like a heartbeat. Marti drew every character by hand.

The interface is a detective notebook: the suspect's file on one page and the evidence on the other, with real SPHEREx images shown as instant photos pinned with paper clips. A rocket travels across the loading bar while the game downloads the data. Instead of reading a result, the player has to earn it: pointing at the suspect, saying which way it moved, and finally answering the question at the heart of the challenge: is it a planet?

TOOLS

Python, pygame, NumPy, Astropy, Astroquery and reproject. Fonts: Patrick Hand and Titillium Web. Slides made in Canva. Background music: "Space" by Kulakovka (Pixabay).

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We used an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) to help write and debug parts of the Python code, to help draft and translate the texts, and to help design the slides. Marti's characters were drawn by hand and then digitized and enhanced with Canva's AI tools. The measurements come from real SPHEREx and SIMBAD data. The voice-over in the demo video was generated with Magnific (AI voice).
